title: China put a 99.2% duty on a chemical chip fabs need
content:
China has imposed a cash deposit of up to 99.2% on imports of a Japanese chemical that chip fabs use to build the films inside logic and memory chips.
The rate is close to prohibitive. It took effect on Tuesday.
China’s Ministry of Commerce published the preliminary determination on 7 September as Announcement No. 37 of 2026. Chan Ho-Him and Mari Yamaguchi reported the ruling and Tokyo’s response for the Associated Press, which describes Japan as the leading producer of ultrapure dichlorosilane for chip fabrication.
What the ruling says
The published rates are not uniform.
Shin-Etsu Chemical draws 99.2%. Denal Silane, a joint venture between Denka and Air Liquide, draws 80.8%. Every other Japanese exporter draws 99.2%.
So the largest supplier gets the top rate, and so does anyone who might replace it.
Dichlorosilane, known in fabs as DCS, feeds chemical vapour deposition. It lays down silicon and oxide films a few atoms thick, layer after layer, in both logic and memory production. It is not exotic. It is a working gas, consumed continuously, and a fab that cannot get it cannot run.
The measure is provisional. The ministry opened the investigation on 7 January, and interested parties have ten days to comment before a final ruling.
One number we cannot give you is Japan’s share of world supply. The figures circulating in market-research summaries contradict each other badly, ranging from under a tenth to three quarters, and none of them cites a primary source. So we are using AP’s wording rather than inventing precision: Japan leads, in a market it calls highly competitive.
This is trade law, not an export control
Here is the part worth noticing.
Beijing has spent two years restricting materials through export controls: gallium, germanium, graphite, rare earths. It also placed curbs on 56 US firms in June. Those measures are unmistakable acts of policy, and they invite retaliation precisely because everyone can see what they are.
An anti-dumping duty looks like something else. It is a trade remedy recognised under WTO rules, available to any member whose domestic producers claim injury from underpriced imports. It comes with a petitioner, an investigation, a determination and a comment period. The European Union used the same instrument against Chinese electric vehicles.
And it produces the same result. A 99.2% deposit at customs stops the goods as effectively as a licence requirement, while looking like ordinary trade defence rather than statecraft.
The dates are worth reading in order
Tangshan Sunfar Electronic Materials, a Chinese producer, filed the application on 8 December 2025.
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi had suggested in November that Japan’s military could intervene in a Taiwan contingency. Relations have been strained since, and Beijing has imposed dual-use export controls on Japanese firms in the months that followed.
We cannot show that one caused the other, and we will not imply it. Anti-dumping petitions take months to prepare, and this one may have been under way before the remarks. What we can say is that it arrived roughly a month after them, and that the determination landed while the dispute was still live.
Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara lodged a protest and said Tokyo would respond appropriately.
The people this hurts most are in China
A duty on imports raises the price for the importer.
Chinese fabs are the ones buying Japanese DCS, and Chinese memory makers are among the heaviest users, because memory stacks far more deposited layers than logic does. CXMT, the country’s largest DRAM producer, is already fighting a US listing in the Washington courts. Its input costs now rise by order of its own government.
That is not an accident. It is what a protective duty is for. Tangshan Sunfar wants the Chinese market, and the ruling hands it over at a price Japanese exporters cannot meet.
Whether Chinese DCS is good enough is a separate question, and the word ultrapure is doing real work in that sentence. Deposition chemistry is unforgiving about contamination, and a fab that switches supplier buys months of qualification work.
Europe buys the chips, not the gas
Memory prices are the transmission channel.
European desktop shipments are already falling because buyers ran out of money, with DRAM up sharply over three quarters. Anything that raises the cost of making memory in China reaches European buyers eventually, through the price of a finished module rather than any shortage of gas.
The reverse effect is also possible and gets less attention. Japanese producers shut out of China have volume to place somewhere. That could make DCS cheaper for fabs in Europe, Taiwan and the United States. Nobody has published numbers on it, so we are raising it as a question rather than a forecast.
Three choke points in one day
This is the third materials story we have written today, and the pattern is the point.
IQE’s chief executive warned that China holds 70% of indium phosphide, the compound underneath the photonics in AI data centres. The Financial Times reported that China’s domestic answer to ASML still runs on Zeiss lenses, a dependency pointing the other way. Now a deposition gas, restricted through trade law.
Different materials, different directions, different legal instruments. What they share is that the contest has moved off finished chips and onto the inputs, where dependencies are older, far less visible, and much harder to substitute in a hurry.
What to watch
Whether the final determination holds the rates. Provisional deposits are refundable if the final ruling goes the other way, which makes this reversible, and therefore usable as leverage rather than as a wall.
Whether Tokyo files at the WTO. Respond appropriately is the phrasing a government reaches for before it has decided.
And whether Chinese fabs report input trouble. That is the number that will show whether Beijing accepted a real cost here, or already had a domestic substitute standing by.

report.summary: 中国对日本产芯片关键气体二氯硅烷征收最高99.2%反倾销保证金。
report.background: 中国商务部应唐山三孚电子材料申请，对原产于日本的二氯硅烷展开反倾销调查，并于2026年9月作出初裁。二氯硅烷是逻辑和存储芯片制造中化学气相沉积的核心气体，日本是全球主要超纯供应商。此前中日因日方涉台言论关系紧张，中国已对日企采取出口管制。此次以反倾销名义实施的近禁止性税率，虽属WTO框架下的贸易救济手段，实际效果却接近出口限制，引发日方抗议，并可能重塑全球芯片材料供应链。
key_points: 反倾销税率接近禁止性：信越化学等日本主要供应商被征收99.2%现金保证金，另一家企业为80.8%，基本封死日本DCS对华出口。
手段选择很讲究：反倾销是WTO认可的贸易救济，比出口管制更具法律正当性，但同样能卡住关键材料，且更难被直接定性为政治报复。
时机耐人寻味：国内厂商在日方涉台言论后约一个月提交申请，初裁时双边争端仍在，但文章强调无法证实直接因果关系。
中国晶圆厂受害最深：长江存储、CXMT等存储厂高度依赖进口DCS，成本抬升后需重新认证国内替代品，耗时数月且存在良率风险。
全球涟漪效应：日本供应商被挡在中国外后可能向其他市场压价出货，而中国内存厂成本上升会推高DRAM价格，最终传导至全球电子产品。
report.impact: 对AI行业而言，AI服务器需要大量高带宽存储和逻辑芯片，材料断供若推高内存价格，将直接增加数据中心建设和推理部署成本。对开发者，云端算力和内存资源价格可能随之上涨，影响AI应用训练与推理的预算。对普通用户，DRAM、闪存等终端产品价格上升会让手机、电脑更贵，短期内难以缓解。全球供应链将加速区域化，各国可能更倾向于囤积关键材料或扶持本土供应商，形成新的技术壁垒。
report.tools: 可关注中国商务部贸易救济信息网（查询案件进展）、WTO争端解决数据库（跟踪日方是否申诉）、SEMI产业报告（获取材料供需数据），以及信越化学、Denka财报和投资者材料研判产能动向。
